findings.title: The new 'one fixture covers both' clause prescribes the fixture the same row calls FRAGILE, and its 'applyChain second' half is false: LocalSequencer.start seals epoch 3 before crossing into it, so applyChain returns at that Seal and never reaches a ckpt key
findings.detail: The clause reads: 'One fixture covers both if epoch 4's Seal@0 already exists when the new leader starts: firstInheritableAncestor then steps over 4 to 3 and recoverChainEnd runs against the checkpoint-bearing chain -- chainEnd first, applyChain second.' The first half checks out: ChainReplay.firstInheritableAncestor (ChainReplay.java:297-306) returns 3 because neverOpened(Seal@0, atOrigin=true) is true at 4 and firstEntry(3) is a Continue, and LocalSequencer.java:238 then runs recoverChainEnd against epoch 3 -- real chainEnd coverage. The second half does not. LocalSequencer.java:239 unconditionally seals that same predecessor (`prevSeq = predecessor.seal(epoch, sealRedriveBudget).sequence()`) BEFORE open() crosses into it, and CommitLog.seal writes at keyFor(nextSequence), i.e. a `<seq:016x>.delta` key, which sorts before `ckpt/`. The only applyChain runs in that takeover are (a) log.recover() at LocalSequencer.java:254 over the still-EMPTY epoch 5, which lists nothing, and (b) open() -> crossFrom -> ChainReplay.inherited over hop (3, sealSeq), where applyChain (ChainReplay.java:331-340) hits `entry instanceof Seal` and returns before the listing ever reaches the ckpt/ keys. So no checkpoint-shaped key is ever read at the applyChain site in this fixture -- which is precisely the trap the same row spells out two clauses earlier ('seal epoch 3 by accident and the hop becomes bounded, applyChain returns at the Seal, and a chainEnd-only fix passes green'), except that here it is not by accident: start always seals the inheritable ancestor. The remedy is cheap and does not need the ancestry walk at all: seed ONE unsealed checkpoint-bearing chain and drive both entry points against it directly -- recover() first (applyChain, the simple shape the row already prefers) and recoverChainEnd() while the chain is still unsealed (chainEnd) -- i.e. the stated order is the wrong way round, because the takeover that gives chainEnd its fixture is what destroys applyChain's.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer picks M4.8b1, reads the row, and takes the economical option the row explicitly offers -- 'One fixture covers both'. They build the epoch-3/epoch-4-Seal@0/epoch-5 takeover, watch it go red (recoverChainEnd reads the ckpt key as the chain end and throws), add the allow-list to ChainReplay.chainEnd ONLY, and go green: the applyChain listing in that same test stops at the Seal the takeover just wrote, so nothing there ever sees a ckpt key. M4.8b1 lands with one of its two mandated sites unfiltered. M4.8b2 then ships the writer; the next takeover whose predecessor chain is unsealed (a leader that died without being sealed -- exactly the neverOpened path this codebase already carries a branch for) crosses into it, applyChain reads a `ckpt/<seq>.ckpt` key, ChainEntry.decode throws on the BCKP magic, start releases the lease, and the next node repeats -- the permanent takeover failure this row opens with, shipped by a row that was rewritten in this very commit to prevent it. This is round 2's tr-11 ('the fix swapped WHICH site is untested') recurring in the opposite direction.

findings.title: The cap argument's two summary claims about its own rounds are not what .harness/review holds: 'fifteen' findings across two rounds is 25 (12 of them major), and 'EVERY FINDING WAS A ROW PRESCRIBING A TEST THAT WOULD NOT DISCRIMINATE' is contradicted by the findings and by the next sentence of the same entry
findings.detail: Counted from .harness/review by task: hash a0a6d968 carries 6 reviewer findings (F1-F3 major, F4-F6 minor) and 10 test-reviewer findings (TR1-TR7 major, TR8-TR10 minor); hash 47aca694 carries 4 reviewer minors (F7-F10) and 5 test-reviewer findings (tr-11, tr-12 major; tr-13..tr-15 minor). That is 25 findings, of which 12 are major -- 'fifteen' matches neither total, neither round, and neither severity class. And the universal is false on its own record: F1 was a missing hard-dependency clause, F2 was cost arithmetic an implementer would size from, F7 a stale cross-reference, F8 a bound stated about the wrong quantity, F10 an ADR mischaracterisation -- none of them a prescribed test that would not discriminate. The entry's own next sentence says so ('The two that matter most were both MY CLAIMS ABOUT THE CODE, not about the tests'), so the paragraph contradicts itself one clause apart. Both are cheap to fix in place: name the classes rather than counting them, as M4.38 and M4.43 already learned to do, or quote the measured 25/12.
findings.failure_scenario: baselines/review.txt is read by later sessions that have only .harness, and its worth is that its entries are checkable -- its own rounds:M4.43 entry is about numbers reported as measurements and about a row that said 'the two minors' when four were recorded. A future session sizing how much review a decomposition costs reads 'fifteen across two rounds' and 'every finding was a non-discriminating test criterion', concludes that decomposition review finds only test-criterion defects at about seven per round, and builds the next split's review brief around that -- missing that a third of the real findings were false claims about production code, which is the class that produced both of round 2's majors.
